name: Delhi
blurb: Seven historic cities layered into one modern capital, Delhi's Mughal-era monuments sit within a short walk of some of India's busiest bazaars.

districts.name: Central Delhi
districts.blurb: Old Delhi's historic core, built around Shah Jahan's 17th-century walled capital.

places.name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
places.blurb: The main residence of the Mughal emperors for over two centuries, a massive red-sandstone fort from whose ramparts India's Prime Minister still addresses the nation every Independence Day.
places.bestPhoto: The Lahori Gate façade at sunset from across the moat garden
places.history: Built as the main residence of the Mughal emperors, commissioned by Shah Jahan in 1638 when he shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to the newly founded city of Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi); it remained the ceremonial and political centre of Mughal power until 1857, after which the British repurposed much of the complex for military use.
places.architecture: A massive red sandstone fort following an octagonal plan, blending Persian, Timurid, and earlier Indian architectural traditions, containing palaces, halls (including the marble Diwan-i-Khas, "Hall of Private Audience"), and formal gardens laid out on Mughal charbagh principles.

timeline.label: Fort completed, becoming the seat of Mughal power.
British forces take control after the Indian Rebellion of 1857; much of the interior is later demolished or repurposed.
India's first Prime Minister raises the national flag here on Independence Day, a tradition continued annually.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts: The Prime Minister of India delivers the Independence Day address from its ramparts every August 15.
Roughly two-thirds of the original interior structures were demolished or altered under British military occupation.
The Peacock Throne, one of history's most famous jeweled thrones, was originally housed here before being carried off in a 1739 invasion.
hiddenGems: Chandni Chowk's old lanes just outside the fort walls
Salimgarh Fort, an older fortification connected to the Red Fort complex
The sound-and-light show held on the fort grounds most evenings
food: Old Delhi street food at Chandni Chowk (parathas, chaat)
Karim's, a historic Mughlai restaurant near Jama Masjid
experiences: Evening sound-and-light show retelling Mughal history
Old Delhi heritage walk from the fort to Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk
Museum galleries within the fort complex

travel.parking: Limited nearby; Delhi Metro (Lal Qila / Chandni Chowk stations) is more reliable
travel.tip: Combine with Chandni Chowk and Jama Masjid in the same outing — all three are within easy walking distance.

places.name: Jama Masjid
places.blurb: India's largest mosque, raised on a rocky ridge above Old Delhi, its courtyards holding twenty-five thousand worshippers beneath three marble domes.
places.open: 7 AM–noon, 1:30 PM–6:30 PM (closed to tourists during prayer)
places.bestPhoto: The domes and minarets from the northeastern parapet at dawn
places.history: Shah Jahan's final architectural act, completed in 1656 as the imperial mosque of his new capital Shahjahanabad. Its architect Austad Ahmad built the emperor's vision on a natural outcrop above the city, and for two centuries its Friday sermon stood at the centre of Delhi's public life — through the 1857 uprising, the end of the Mughals and the making of modern Delhi all around it.
places.architecture: A vast courtyard of red sandstone entered by three gateways, with an eleven-arched prayer hall faced in white marble strips that read as devotional calligraphy from a distance. Two minarets rise 40 metres, and the central courtyards hold a marble pulpit and ablution tank on a single axis pointed at Mecca.

timeline.label: The mosque opens with imperial ceremony.
The uprising damages the complex; it survives retribution.
A conservation programme restores the courtyard and domes.

facts: The courtyard holds up to 25,000 worshippers at once.
It was the last of Shah Jahan's great buildings, finished 20 years after the Red Fort.
The eastern gateway was reserved for the emperor alone.
hiddenGems: The southern minaret climb for a rooftop view over Chandni Chowk and the Red Fort
The food lanes of Matia Mahal immediately outside the south gate
The ablution tank at dawn when the courtyard is empty
food: Karim's, a stone's throw from the gate, a Delhi institution since 1913
Biryani and korma in the Matia Mahal bazaar lanes
experiences: Climbing a minaret for the Old Delhi skyline
Sitting in the courtyard as the maghrib prayer call rings out
A food walk from the mosque gates through Chandni Chowk

travel.railway: Old Delhi Railway Station, 3 km; New Delhi, 6 km
travel.parking: Scarce; the Metro to Jama Masjid or Chandni Chowk station is far easier
travel.tip: Time your visit between prayer hours — tourists are turned away during namaaz, and Fridays are busiest.

places.name: Humayun's Tomb
places.blurb: The first great garden tomb of the Mughals — a red sandstone and marble landmark that taught India the Taj Mahal's grammar a century early.
places.bestPhoto: The tomb across its water channels from the west gate at golden hour
places.history: Begun in 1565 by Humayun's widow Bega Begum, nearly a decade after the emperor's death, it was the first structure in India to use the Persian charbagh tomb-garden at monumental scale. Its architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas brought the double-dome technique from Herat, and when Shah Jahan's architects sought a model for the Taj Mahal a century later, this is what they studied.
places.architecture: A 47-metre-high double dome of white marble crowns a red sandstone body with white inlay borders, raised on a vast terraced platform split by water channels. The tomb holds the emperor's cenotaph in a vaulted chamber of exactly-graded proportions, and the surrounding garden once held the tombs of an entire dynasty.

timeline.label: The last Mughal emperor is captured here by British forces.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A twelve-year restoration returns the gardens and fountains to working order.

facts: It was the first garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent.
The Taj Mahal's architects clearly studied its double dome and charbagh plan.
The restoration was the largest ever undertaken by the Aga Khan Trust.
hiddenGems: Isa Khan's tomb in the same enclosure — an older, octagonal Lodi-era gem most visitors walk past
The barber's tomb on the plinth's southeast corner
Sundar Nursery next door, a restored Mughal-era garden complex
food: Lajpat Nagar market chaat, a short drive south
Nizamuddin's galouti kebabs near the dargah
experiences: Walking the restored water channels at golden hour
Finding Isa Khan's tomb first, before the main structure
Pairing the tomb with Sundar Nursery in one long morning

travel.parking: At Sundar Nursery and on Mathura Road; the JLN Stadium Metro is 2 km
travel.tip: Enter at 6 AM opening — the light on the sandstone is at its best and the lawns are empty.

places.name: Qutub Minar
places.blurb: A 73-metre sandstone minaret begun in 1193, ringed with calligraphy bands, standing in a compound that holds Delhi's oldest mosque and a rust-proof iron pillar sixteen centuries old.
places.bestPhoto: The minar framed by the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque arches
places.history: Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the tower in 1193 to mark the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate — the first Muslim kingdom in north India — and his successor Iltutmish added three more storeys. Lightning and repairs altered the top over the centuries, and the compound's Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque was expanded by successive sultans, its pillars reused from dozens of demolished Hindu and Jain temples.
places.architecture: Five tapering storeys, each ringed by projecting balconies on corbelled brackets, with bands of incised Arabic calligraphy running around every stage. The compound also holds the Alai Darwaza gatehouse — a masterpiece of early Islamic architecture in India — an incomplete second minar, and the almost unchanged Iron Pillar of the 4th century, standing in the mosque courtyard.

timeline.label: Aibak begins the minaret to mark the new Sultanate.
Firoz Shah rebuilds the top after lightning damage.
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts: At 73 metres it was among the tallest towers on Earth when built.
The Iron Pillar has resisted rust for some 1,600 years — a metallurgical puzzle.
The Alai Minar next door was meant to be twice this height, but only its base was built.
hiddenGems: The Alai Darwaza's carved dome ceiling, easy to miss in the corner of the compound
Graves of the madrasa in the northwest of the complex
Mehrauli Archaeological Park beyond the gate — centuries of ruins with almost no crowds
food: Mehrauli's kebabs and Mughlai fare near the entrance
Sohna Road cafés a short drive away for a sit-down meal
experiences: Reading the calligraphy bands storey by storey from the ground
Testing the Iron Pillar legend with your back to it, hands behind
An afternoon in Mehrauli Archaeological Park after the compound

travel.railway: Hazrat Nizamuddin, 10 km; New Delhi, 14 km
travel.parking: Paid lot outside the entrance; the Qutub Minar Metro station is 2 km
travel.tip: Go early morning or late afternoon — the compound has no shade and midday light flattens the sandstone carvings.
